subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER    REFERENCE TO REPORTED SPEECH BY PRIME MINISTER

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER    REFERENCE TO REPORTED SPEECH BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege arising out of a report in the Montreal Star of March 17, 1962 of a speech made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) reflecting on the conduct of members of the opposition in this house. I should like to read the following extract from that paper:
Prime Minister Diefenbaker in a Montreal address last night criticized delaying tactics which he said were holding up passage of important legislation.
By needless debate of the government's supplementary estimates, he claimed, Liberal members were blocking "legislative enactments we wish to place on the country's statute books."
The Prime Minister laid the blame on a "small group of Liberals in the house-"
That statement is not in accordance with the facts. For example on Thursday of last week, as Your Honour knows, after the Minister of Finance-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER    REFERENCE TO REPORTED SPEECH BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: Order. The hon. member need not refer to what happened in the house, as that is common knowledge, and furthermore that matter was disposed of at the time. If the hon. member sees a question of privilege affecting members in the remarks as reported, perhaps he could give me some authority or precedent for the proposition he makes.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER    REFERENCE TO REPORTED SPEECH BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
First of all I should like to add another statement which substantiates what I have said. Then I shall be glad to give Your Honour some authority. The Prime Minister went on further to say this, and I quote his words:
"Now," he declared, "we have been held up 14 days by fruitless talk designed to delay the country's affairs. I welcome full discussion but not mere repetition. I don't know the reason. I'll leave the answer to you."
That is an inaccurate statement, because they have not been held up for 14 days.
Then, sir, to come to the point which you raised and which affects the privileges of the opposition in this free parliament, it is this. When the Prime Minister seeks by statements outside the house, which are not supported by the facts, to restrict freedom of debate within the house-and according to the 26207-1-121
same press report that is what the Prime Minister was trying to do-I do not think the rules of the house permit the Prime Minister to make these reflections upon the members of the opposition, particularly having regard to the fact that the Minister of Finance indicated clearly that consideration of these estimates should be completed by the middle of the month, the Prime Minister himself said they should be completed by the end of the month, and the house leader said that they-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER    REFERENCE TO REPORTED SPEECH BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Order. The hon. member's discussion of the matter is, I think, ranging unnecessarily widely. The point he makes is that there is a breach of privilege if an hon. member makes statements outside of the house that are critical of the conduct of members in the house. I have no recollection that such an outside speech has been held in the past such as to raise a question of privilege, particularly where it was a general imputation against a group and not critical of an individual; nor is there anything in the report of the speech from which the hon. member has read to indicate that what was imputed to members of the opposition generally was something which would be morally improper or wrong.
There have been a good many instances in the house when members on both sides have accused those on the other side of blocking legislation, and that has not generally been held to be improper even when said in the house. Therefore unless the hon. member can find some precedent for the point he raises, it seems to me that he would have difficulty making out a case of infringement of the privileges of the house. Perhaps the party involved, the Prime Minister, would like to comment on the point raised.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER    REFERENCE TO REPORTED SPEECH BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: May I complete my point? Your Honour has asked me to give you a precedent. I think a precedent has been established by Your Honour, because what in effect the Prime Minister was doing was repeating outside the house what Your Honour rebuked the Prime Minister for doing inside the house; because Your Honour-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER    REFERENCE TO REPORTED SPEECH BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Order. Before the hon. member proceeds, may I say that in my view the circumstances there were quite different. What was objected to there was a remark made following an answer to a question, a

Question of Privilege
remark made in the house that was related obviously to the conduct of the members who were then asking questions-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER    REFERENCE TO REPORTED SPEECH BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: Concerning the business of the house.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER    REFERENCE TO REPORTED SPEECH BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: -and in my view that charge or imputation then made was not a proper one to be introduced into an answer to a question. If it had been a general observation that the opposition was employing tactics which were obstructing the procedure of the house I would not have found that objectionable because that has been done from time to time, and, although it is not desirable it is not something that has been regarded as a breach of privilege. Unless the hon. member has a further precedent, I consider that to be a distinguishable circumstance.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER    REFERENCE TO REPORTED SPEECH BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: May I be allowed to give this additional precedent? The statement made by the Prime Minister outside the house was not factual; it was not in accordance with the facts.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER    REFERENCE TO REPORTED SPEECH BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I now give the facts? On supplementary estimates in-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER    REFERENCE TO REPORTED SPEECH BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: Order. Before the Prime Minister proceeds, may I indicate that what is before the house is a question of privilege, and I do not think the question of privilege is to be disposed of on a verification of the facts as to the circumstances which give rise to the question of privilege. The question of whether what the Prime Minister is alleged to have said actually was said is a fact that is relevant; and if it was said, whether it then raised any matter of privilege. I would not consider it appropriate to attempt to establish the fact of whether or not the opposition has been employing tactics which are delaying.

subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER    REFERENCE TO REPORTED SPEECH BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
With the greatest of
respect, Mr. Speaker, you have allowed the hon. gentleman to make statements that are not in accordance with the facts, and I want to clarify the record so there will be no doubt.

subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER    REFERENCE TO REPORTED SPEECH BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: Speak to the question of privilege. On a point of order, Mr. Speaker-

subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER    REFERENCE TO REPORTED SPEECH BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: I think I have the floor now.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER    REFERENCE TO REPORTED SPEECH BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: If the point of order relates to what the Prime Minister is about to say I will hear it.

subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER    REFERENCE TO REPORTED SPEECH BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, you have made a ruling that the right hon. gentleman may speak to this matter in so far as it

involves a question of privilege. The right hon. gentleman now is about to ignore your ruling and is doing the very thing Your Honour said he should not do.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER    REFERENCE TO REPORTED SPEECH BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: The hon. member knows more about what the right hon. gentleman is about to say than I do, then. The Prime Minister is at liberty to deal with matters brought forward by the hon. member for Laurier. This is one of the basic rules of debate. The only matter about which I was cautioning the Prime Minister was not to become involved, as I thought he might be from his opening sentence, in an attempt to demonstrate factually what the conduct of the opposition has been.

subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER    REFERENCE TO REPORTED SPEECH BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: Were I to rise on a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker, every time I saw a statement the opposition made outside of the house which was not in accordance with the facts, we would not get very much business done. I do not follow that course. However, in view of the statements made by the hon. gentleman, I think I will let the record answer him.

subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER    REFERENCE TO REPORTED SPEECH BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: Order. The Prime Minister is now seeking to do what you said a few minutes ago, Mr. Speaker, he could not do.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER    REFERENCE TO REPORTED SPEECH BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: Order. As I recall it, the hon. member for Laurier, in his statement, said that what the opposition was accused of was not true. It seems to me it would be improper to prevent the Prime Minister from replying.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER    REFERENCE TO REPORTED SPEECH BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: Your Honour did not give me an opportunity to prove that what was said by the Prime Minister was untrue. I wanted to do that, but Your Honour interrupted me. Now Your Honour is giving the Prime Minister the right to put the facts on the record. I have facts here, and I think my facts are equally as accurate as those which the Prime Minister intends to produce.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER    REFERENCE TO REPORTED SPEECH BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: Before the Prime Minister proceeds, may I say this. In my opinion there is no question of privilege involved in the facts which have been brought forward by the hon. member for Laurier. However, certain statements have been made, and I think it is only proper that the Prime Minister should have the opportunity to controvert those statements. I would hope that he would keep himself within that category.

subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER    REFERENCE TO REPORTED SPEECH BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: On the point of order-

subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER    REFERENCE TO REPORTED SPEECH BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER    REFERENCE TO REPORTED SPEECH BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: I find great difficulty in putting these facts before the house.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER    REFERENCE TO REPORTED SPEECH BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
I think the point of order has been sufficiently dealt with, and the course

should be to give the Prime Minister an opportunity to reply. He has not yet had an opportunity to say what he has to say.

subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER    REFERENCE TO REPORTED SPEECH BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: I think the facts will speak for themselves, and that may be the reason for the points of order that are being raised so indiscriminately. In 1962 the number of days spent on supplementary estimates up to March 16 was 14. I now take a period of time while we were in opposition to set out a comparison in 1952-53, one day-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER    REFERENCE TO REPORTED SPEECH BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: Order. I think the Prime Minister has misunderstood me, because if he continued in that vein he would really be debating the issue of whether or not the conduct of the opposition amounts to obstruction. I do not consider that that point is in issue. The question that was raised was whether there had been a breach of the privileges of the house in what the Prime Minister had said, to the effect that he is now endeavouring to substantiate. The substantiation of what the Prime Minister said would, to my mind, be irrelevant. It opens a debate on the conduct of the opposition rather than on a question of privilege. I had only given the Prime Minister the floor to comment as far as was necessary on the charges that were made by the hon. member for Laurier.

subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER    REFERENCE TO REPORTED SPEECH BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: I do not know how I can answer the allegations without placing the facts before the house, and I simply want to point out certain facts, that in the period from 1952-53-

subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER    REFERENCE TO REPORTED SPEECH BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: Order.

subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER    REFERENCE TO REPORTED SPEECH BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, you have ruled on the point; you have ruled that the Prime Minister cannot continue, and the Prime Minister continues to defy that ruling. He should be the first one in this house to obey your ruling.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER    REFERENCE TO REPORTED SPEECH BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: You don't want the truth.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER    REFERENCE TO REPORTED SPEECH BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
The hon. member must at least allow enough latitude until the tenor of the Prime Minister's remarks is apparent. I had indicated to the Prime Minister that an attempt, by the introduction of other evidence, to demonstrate that what has happened amounts to delaying tactics was irrelevant. I think that is the correct view. The Prime Minister is at liberty to comment on what has taken place here in this house in this session, insofar as it has been raised by the hon. member for Laurier, but I would consider it improper to go beyond that to endeavour to establish, by comparison and debate, that fact which is not really at issue.
26207-1-121*
Question of Privilege

subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER    REFERENCE TO REPORTED SPEECH BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: With the greatest of respect, Mr. Speaker, I do not know how I can answer such an obviously transparent suggestion by the opposition that a question of privilege arises. I point out with great deference, that in the period of five years between 1952 and 1956, supplementary estimates took nine days.

subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER    REFERENCE TO REPORTED SPEECH BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: Order.

subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER    REFERENCE TO REPORTED SPEECH BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: Defying the Speaker again.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER    REFERENCE TO REPORTED SPEECH BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: Order. We must allow the hon. member reasonable latitude to make his point. He has to express his view.

subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER    REFERENCE TO REPORTED SPEECH BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: The total number of days taken up on supplementary estimates was nine days, for five years.

subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER    REFERENCE TO REPORTED SPEECH BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: Why not 1957?

subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER    REFERENCE TO REPORTED SPEECH BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: I appreciate the position Your Honour is in, trying to accommodate both sides with a sense of fairness, but Your Honour has made a ruling and the Prime Minister has now twice, in my judgment, defied that ruling. If it is felt that there should be a discussion of this matter on the merits there is a procedure open to the house, and that is to allow both sides to discuss the merits of the question. But the Prime Minister, although he is the leader of the house, has now risen for the second time and each time he has risen he has defied your ruling.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER    REFERENCE TO REPORTED SPEECH BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: I think perhaps the hon. member has some justification for his point, but I suggest to him that he is prejudging the issue. The Prime Minister must be given some latitude to deal with the matter in his own discretion. I have indicated the lines which I think are appropriate, and I am sure the house will give the Prime Minister an opportunity to comment, as he is entitled to do, on what was said by the hon. member for Laurier, without being unduly restrictive and sensitive. If I find that it goes beyond what I consider to be the appropriate course, I shall take the necessary steps.

subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER    REFERENCE TO REPORTED SPEECH BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: On that, Mr. Speaker, I am simply pointing out that the hon. gentlemen's sensibilities axe easily aroused. A statement has been made that I said something that apparently was unfair.

subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER    REFERENCE TO REPORTED SPEECH BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: No; untrue.

subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER    REFERENCE TO REPORTED SPEECH BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
What I did was simply point out that in a period of five years, when we were equally careful in examining estimates, we used up nine days on supplementary estimates, and so far 14 days have been used up by the opposition this session. I can only repeat, having read each

Question of Privilege
and every line of what has been said, that it is very apparent that repetition is not foreign to the opposition. Over and over again they have said the same things. More than that I need not say.

subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER    REFERENCE TO REPORTED SPEECH BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: Listen to the master calling.

subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER    REFERENCE TO REPORTED SPEECH BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Compared with what
happened over that period of five years, what is happening in this session of parliament drives anyone who gives it consideration to a conclusion which I am prepared to accept.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER    REFERENCE TO REPORTED SPEECH BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: Mr. Speaker-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER    REFERENCE TO REPORTED SPEECH BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: I do not know whether or not the hon. member for Kootenay West wishes to intervene on this point-

subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER    REFERENCE TO REPORTED SPEECH BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER    REFERENCE TO REPORTED SPEECH BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: If not, I will hear the hon. member for Laurier.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER    REFERENCE TO REPORTED SPEECH BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: On what subject?

subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER    REFERENCE TO REPORTED SPEECH BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: On the merits now. We are going to have a debate.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER    REFERENCE TO REPORTED SPEECH BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Prime
Minister has said that he has been accused, by the statement which I raised on a question of privilege, that what he said in Montreal was unfair. That is not what I said; I said that the statement made by the Prime Minister was untrue, and I would like to prove that the statement he made was untrue, since he took time to deal with exactly the same thing by putting on the record some of the facts which he said he had.
We know very well what happened in this house on Thursday. On Thursday there was far more time taken up by hon. members on the other side of the house than there was by hon. members on this side of the house.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER    REFERENCE TO REPORTED SPEECH BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Order. I think the hon. member for Laurier will agree, and I am sure the house has come to the conclusion by this time, that we are engaged in a perfectly fruitless debate. The hon. member for Laurier did, as was his right, raise objection to what was said on the basis that it involved a matter of privilege. In my view it does not raise a breach of the privileges of the house. There has been some debate on both sides as to the merits of the accusation which, as I said, is not relevant. We can go on and have a first class debate on that issue, but it would be entirely irregular and out of order.
If the hon. member for Laurier has nothing further to add except to demonstrate the propriety of the conduct of the opposition, I suggest that he do it by letting us get on with the work of the house.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER    REFERENCE TO REPORTED SPEECH BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: I have something more, Mr. Speaker. The Prime Minister has said that 14 days were taken up. That is not a fact. We have been dealing with further supplementary estimates No. 3 since the 8th day of March. That is seven days-

subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER    REFERENCE TO REPORTED SPEECH BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: What about group No. 2?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER    REFERENCE TO REPORTED SPEECH BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: -and not 14 days, as the Prime Minister said. As we well know, we were told by the Minister of Finance, first, that these supplementary estimates No. 3 had to be passed and disposed of by March 15. We were then told by the Prime Minister in this speech in Montreal that they had to be completed by the end of the month.

subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER    REFERENCE TO REPORTED SPEECH BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER    REFERENCE TO REPORTED SPEECH BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: Then the leader of the house felt they were of such little urgency that it was not necessary to go on with supplementary estimates today; he announced on Friday that we should go on with legislation. So that we have three degrees of urgency; that laid down by the Minister of Finance, which was very urgent; that laid down by the Prime Minister, which was less urgent, and that laid down by the leader of the house, which was that there was no urgency at all because we would go on with legislation on Monday.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER    REFERENCE TO REPORTED SPEECH BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: Order. I recognize the Minister of Finance. Those other hon. members who wish to speak might send notice to the Chair.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER    REFERENCE TO REPORTED SPEECH BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I hope I can contribute to the calm which reigns sometimes in this chamber.

subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER    REFERENCE TO REPORTED SPEECH BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: You can do that best by not speaking.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER    REFERENCE TO REPORTED SPEECH BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: What I said last week concerning the urgency of the disposal of the supplementary estimates then under discussion in committee of supply was absolutely correct, as I do not need to say. The carrying of those estimates to a decision is highly urgent. I pointed out the reasons that payments are being delayed because we have no authority to make them, payments to contractors and also payment of wages in certain cases.

subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER    REFERENCE TO REPORTED SPEECH BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: That is not what you said the other day.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER    REFERENCE TO REPORTED SPEECH BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
That was the situation. The discussion of these estimates went on an additional day, an eighth day, last Friday, and one item had been passed in that period. In the eight days 22 items have been passed.

The 14 days that were referred to by the Prime Minister were six days spent on supplementary estimates No. 2 and now eight days spent on supplementary estimates No. 3, and of the latter we have so far carried in committee of supply only 22, a minority of them, and there are still many items to be carried.
I have indicated that there will be more estimates to be brought down, the final supplementary estimates for the year. What the Prime Minister referred to as estimates requiring to be passed by the end of the month are all those supplementary estimates including those which I hope to introduce a little later.
And as for the announcement made by my colleague the leader of the house last Friday, in all fairness the house well knows that the only reason the Minister of Veterans Affairs announced on that occasion that we would be taking legislation today instead of proceeding with the supplementary estimates is that he had simply come to the conclusion that it was hopeless to expect to get any of these estimates passed, and he was hopeful, then, that with a change-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER    REFERENCE TO REPORTED SPEECH BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER    REFERENCE TO REPORTED SPEECH BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: The hon. member interrupts me when I am seeking to contribute to good will in the chamber.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER    REFERENCE TO REPORTED SPEECH BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: Order.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER    REFERENCE TO REPORTED SPEECH BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question of privilege is this-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER    REFERENCE TO REPORTED SPEECH BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: Order. I am sorry, but we have not disposed of the first question of privilege yet, and I cannot entertain a second one until this is disposed of.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER    REFERENCE TO REPORTED SPEECH BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: I had nearly finished, Mr. Speaker. I hope the hon. member for Laurier realizes that I was speaking reasonably and trying to contribute to calm and good will in the house.

subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER    REFERENCE TO REPORTED SPEECH BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: What a change.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER    REFERENCE TO REPORTED SPEECH BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
The announcement made on Friday by my colleague the leader of the house did not subtract anything whatsoever from the urgency which the government attaches to these estimates and the urgency of the plea I made to the whole house in relation to the passage of those estimates when I made that plea last Thursday. It was simply that we had come to the point where we thought it was apparent we could not get any of the estimates passed, and my colleague thought that with a change of business for today there perhaps would be some
Railway Act
sense of order and some sense of desire reestablished to proceed with the business of the house.
This is extremely urgent business, and it is becoming more and more urgent with the passage of each day. I simply renew the appeal I made to all parties in the house last Thursday.

subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER    REFERENCE TO REPORTED SPEECH BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think we would be more impressed by what has been said by the Minister of Finance if he had taken some cognizance of the offer made by my friend the hon. member for Laurier, which will be found on page 1900 of Hansard of Friday, that if the minister would indicate in detail what those urgent items were the opposition would be prepared to deal with them immediately and facilitate an appropriation bill which would meet the immediate needs of the government without restricting the rights of the opposition, and that courteous offer has not even been replied to by the government.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER    REFERENCE TO REPORTED SPEECH BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: We will proceed with the business of the order paper, and when we reach the item "motions", if there is anything further to be said about the business of the house we will renew the discussion then.

A message from His Excellency the Governor General transmitting supplementary estimates for the financial year ending March 31, 1962, was presented by Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance), read by Mr. Speaker to the house, and referred to the committee of supply.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF SUBMISSION RESPECTING SECTION 182

speechtext:
On the order: Government notices of motion:
March 15-The Minister of Transport-The following proposed motion:-
That the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines be empowered to examine and inquire into a submission which has been addressed to the chairman of the committee by the national legislative committee, International Railway Brotherhoods, concerning the provisions of section 182 of the Railway Act and suggesting changes in the said section which would provide for the payment of compensation to employees affected by line abandonments; or by the closing or removal of any station or divisional point; or by the changing of operating centres or terminal points.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF SUBMISSION RESPECTING SECTION 182
speechtext:

Questions
(Questions answered orally are indicated by an asterisk.)

subtopic: *C.N.R. BUS SERVICE, FORT-WILLIAM-LONGLAC
*C.N.R. BUS SERVICE, FORT-WILLIAM-LONGLAC
speechtext:
1.	Have any of the officials of the Canadian National Railways been negotiating with Greyhound bus lines or any other bus lines with a view to a sale, lease, or rent of the bus service presently being carried on by the C.N.R. between Fort William and Longlac, Ontario; and, (a) if not, is the railway giving any consideration to making any efforts to sell this bus route (b) if so, at what stage in the negotiations is the principle being held to by the C.N.R. that the security and pensions of the employees on this line are protected?
2.	Does the C.N.R. consider that this bus service, alone and in unison with express and other truck service, is a profitable one?
3.	Who has been carrying on negotiations?
4.	Does the price for such a sale, and/or the equipment, have to pass the scrutiny of both the board of transport commissioners and the cabinet?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: *C.N.R. BUS SERVICE, FORT-WILLIAM-LONGLAC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Canadian National Railways advise as follows:
1.	Negotiations are in progress, and should a sale of the service take place the labour agreement under which the employees operate stipulates the rights of the employees in the particular circumstances.
2.	The bus service was established in the first instance in substitution for train service thereby producing a less expensive operation.

subtopic: SMUGGLING BY MEMBERS OF COMMISSIONS
speechtext:
The answer is as follows:
l.(a) Immediately upon receipt of information about improper activities on the part of certain members of the international

Questions
supervisory commission staff, an investigation was instituted and the individuals concerned were brought back to Canada to be questioned by the appropriate authorities. Written confessions were obtained from them and they were suspended from the Department of External Affairs, pending final investigations and dismissal. Under Canadian law dismissal is the extent of the punishment which can be given in the case of these two men.
The Department of Justice and the Department of External Affairs have been considering the extension of extraterritorial jurisdiction over Canadian government employees abroad. Last summer the commission on uniformity of legislation, consisting of the assistant deputy attorneys general or senior solicitors of the provinces examined this proposal, and detailed legislation is now being prepared to amend the Criminal Code in this respect.
(b) There was no question of diplomatic immunity involved in the case of any of the Canadians, civilian or military, who were alleged to have been engaged in smuggling. These activities were discovered by the Canadian authorities and dealt with by them as expeditiously as possible. All those concerned were returned to Canada where a full scale investigation into the allegations made against them could be carried out.
The local authorities made no representations to the Canadian authorities concerning these allegations and therefore the question of their liability under the laws of another country has never been raised.

River): Mr. Speaker, I should like to address a question to the Minister of Finance. Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of
Finance): Mr. Speaker, assuming that you regard this lengthy question as one that is proper on the orders of the day, let me begin by taking up the remark of the hon. member about sermons. I was not aware that I had been preaching any sermons on this subject but believe me, Mr. Speaker, if the time ever comes when I take to preaching sermons there is nobody who could better absorb them than the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River.
The answer I gave the hon. member on the occasion to which he has referred is quite correct. There has been no change in policy. After Mr. Rasminsky had taken over his duties last summer as governor of the bank he met with representatives of a number of leading investment houses in Canada and proposed to them that for the time being it would be desirable that they should not undertake financing in the United States market, with the opportunities that existed in Canada for that purpose. It was expected that this would

Inquiries of the Ministry be for a temporary period and, in the view of the governor, that period has now been concluded. 669. To authorize the Minister of Finance, notwithstanding the Unemployment Insurance Act, to credit to the unemployment insurance fund in the fiscal year 1962-63 sums not exceeding in the aggregate $25 million on such terms and conditions as the governor in council determines, $25,000,000.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask the minister or his parliamentary assistant a question or two in connection with this item. speechtext: I will get that information for the hon. member.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: While the officials of the department are coming down, perhaps I could put another question I have in mind.
