maintopic: STUDY OF MEASURES TO LIMIT ELECTION CAMPAIGN EXPENDITURES
STUDY OF MEASURES TO LIMIT ELECTION CAMPAIGN EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
That a special committee, consisting of sixteen members to be designated later, be appointed to consider and recommend means of assuring greater independence to members of parliament through more effective measures to limit and control expenditures in the campaigns for the election of members of the House of Commons, and that standing order 67(1) be suspended in relation thereto.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the motion I am now making is that a special committee of the house be set up. I considered rather carefully whether it should be a special committee or whether it should be the committee on privileges and elections. I may say quite frankly that if someone wished to move, by way of an amendment to my motion, that the matter be remitted to the committee on privileges and elections, I would have no

objection. My experience with that committee in 1960, when we were considering the elections act, was that on the whole it was an excellent committee which, in view of the fact that we were considering the elections act, did its work in an extremely objective and non-partisan way most of the time. Oh, I will admit that there were times when we did not forget that we were party politicians. However, the atmosphere in that committee was as agreeable-and I am sure that many others who served on it can say the same thing-as that in any committee on which I have ever served in the House of Commons. At the time we were considering the elections act, both in the committee and in the debate on the act in the house, I made a few observations along the lines of those I am going to make today. I make my observations today, of course, with a great deal more confidence and, in a sense, with a good deal more authority than I made those of two years ago. The views which I expressed two years ago were just my own views. The views I am going to express today are views that have been formally accepted by the political party to which I belong as a part of its program for action when it is once more called upon by the people of this country to form a government.
It is very simple indeed to put to the house the proposition which I should like to have considered by this special committee and I do not need to take a great deal of the time of the house in order to do so as I should like to have other hon. members express their interest in this matter. I think the real debate and discussion should take place in the special committee itself where we could really get down to cases.
Stated briefly, the proposition relates to two things which are absolutely interconnected and interdependent. Of course, the first one could be done without the other but I doubt that it would ever be done effectively in that way. On the other hand, no responsible parliament would ever do the second one without doing the first. The first is the limitation of the total expenditures permitted both candidates and political parties in general elections and presumably also in by-elections. The second is the payment of the greater part of these expenditures-possibly all of them but certainly the greater part of them-out of the public treasury.
The first proposition I think would meet with almost universal acceptance as a desirable thing in itself. I do not think there are many people in this country who could honestly say they think it is a good idea to have unlimited money spent on election campaigns. However, there are many people who are dubious about the possibility of policing

expenditures. Once you start in this field of prohibition, as everyone knows, difficulties are encountered. It is a very difficult field in which to legislate unless there is a really genuine consensus in the community in favour of prohibition. However, this would not really be complete prohibition. It would be a prohibition of only more than a certain amount of expenditures. What it would really be is temperance rather than prohibition. Of course, everybody is in favour of temperance.
It is true that in the elections act we defined things precisely and we made many changes in the definitions in this parliament in 1960. We defined carefully those things on which money cannot be spent by candidates. However, our constitution really takes little account of political parties. It does so in a few respects in the elections act, but not many. It is, of course, perfectly fruitless to limit the expenditures of individual candidates so long as party expenditures are not limited, in certain fields at any rate. I think this problem has become an urgent one. I think it is much more urgent than it ever was previously and that, with the advent of television, it is much more intractable than it ever was previously. We all know that television is extremely costly. We all know that some measure of use of television is essential if political parties are to compete with all the other demands upon the time and attention of the electorate. Perhaps it would be nicer if that were not so. Perhaps it would be nicer if there were such an ardent flame of patriotism burning in all our people that they would deny themselves all amusements and all other avocations to listen to politicians. But we all know they will not do so; we all know that we will not be listened to or looked at unless we compete with the other shows. With television this becomes increasingly difficult and also increasingly costly.
There is another aspect, of course, of this problem of limitation that is also very important. I think it is impossible to have voluntary limitation. If it were left entirely to the party managers right after each election when they are faced with the cold, hard facts of the bills they have to pay and the difficulties they have in paying them, I feel sure they might reach an agreement about how much they would do, but there would be no sanction to it and in the heat of an election campaign one would always have one's doubts. I frankly confess that in those circumstances 1 would not have enough faith in human nature to believe that it would really work. I think it is like disarmament. I think it has got to have a sanction and the sanction must be the sanction of the law. I believe of course, that if the right kind
Election Campaign Expenditures of penalties and the right kind of enforcement machinery are provided there will be such an enormous incentive to all political parties to abide by the law that in fact it will not be nearly as difficult to enforce as many people think.
A much more revolutionary idea of course, under our system of government is the idea that the expenditures or a large part of them should be paid out of the treasury. Why would anyone advocate that? Why would anyone suggest that this should be done instead of following the present system of raising voluntary, quasi voluntary or perhaps some involuntary contributions from certain sections of the community that want to support a political party or feel impelled for one reason or another to support a political party? In the days before 1900 political campaigns really did not cost very much. If the average candidate could raise a few hundred dollars he could buy a horse and buggy, get around his constituency and attend a few meetings. A free show was being put on and it was fairly easy to raise the necessary funds among the neighbours. But today we are all conscious of the fact that very large sums of money have to be raised for what are perfectly legitimate and proper expenditures and what would be, even with the most rigid limitation, perfectly proper, legitimate and, I think, necessary expenditures if we are to have an informed public exercising the franchise. I do not think anyone would argue seriously that, with the state of the world today, that is not a desirable objective.
Of course, it is easy to enunciate the general principle, but how would this principle be worked out in practice? I have no fixed views upon that. I would be glad to put a scheme forward at any time. I would be happy to put a scheme forward for discussion in the committee but I would not think that I had the final word on this any more, I am sure, than any other hon. member would. I think there are half a dozen ways in which this could be done and fortunately, of course, we are going to have some practical guidance in this matter. As hon. members know, there is a bill before the legislature of one of the provinces to do precisely what I am suggesting we in this house should merely study. There is an actual bill before the legislative assembly of Quebec at the present time having as its objectives what I am suggesting here. I am sure that bill will be changed before it is finally enacted and I am sure any scheme I might put forward in the committee would be changed.
But perhaps, sir, I should indicate the broad general lines on which I think this could be done practically. Basically the amount of

Election Campaign Expenditures money would be in proportion to the number of electors. If another reform which is mentioned in the speech from the throne actually does come about, the number of electors in each constituency, of course, is presumably going to be somewhat less uneven than at the present time. But it would be quite absurd to give someone who represented
18,000	people the same amount to spend as someone who represented 225,000, except perhaps in the Mackenzie River or Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador constituencies where someone representing a very small number of people would perhaps need to have more to cover the area effectively.
So I think two factors would have to be considered. The basic factor would be so many cents or dollars per elector with a division of that sum between the parties and the candidates on some prearranged formula. But I think we would also have to take account of these hinterland areas and there would have to be some special provision made so that candidates in those areas could in fact have the same reasonable access to the electors as candidates in more densely populated areas.
It also seems to me that there would be relatively little difficulty in doing this if there were only two political parties, but I would not argue for a minute, that there should be legislation for only two political parties. I agree with Mr. Stanley Knowles, who was once a very distinguished member of this house, that parliament functions best-I was rather surprised that Mr. Knowles should say this in his book-when there are only two parties; but while we may be approaching that state, though not exactly in the way Mr. Knowles expected us to approach it, we are not going to reach it very quickly. Certainly no member of my party that I have ever heard of, and I would hope no other member of the house, would ever suggest that we should try to limit the country legally to only two political parties. I believe that would be a restriction of liberty that would be quite un-British, if I may put it that way.
It seems to me that if the electors of a country feel they cannot express themselves properly or get representation within the scope of existing political parties they should, if self-government means anything, have the freedom if they want to, to elect people who do not belong to those parties or do not belong to any party. That means that some kind of equitable formula has to be devised in the case where there are third and fourth parties in order to make provision for these parties and also for their candidates. Candidates are much less difficult than parties, I agree, but I do not think this is an insuperable problem.


There is another problem, of course, which exists perhaps more in some provinces than in others, but does exist. I refer to what might be called the nuisance candidate, the person who presents himself for election to advertise his business or just out of sheer exhibitionism, or is perhaps somewhat stimulated to do so because his name is exactly like the name of one of the other candidates and it is felt that if he is encouraged to offer himself as a candidate he may deform the results of the election. Of course, I think there are two things that ought to be done about that situation. One of them is that we should require more real electors to sign the candidates' papers and the deposit should be increased. I advocated this change in the committee on privileges and elections without success, though I think there was a lot of sympathy for the view I expressed.
It seems to me that these exhibitionists of one sort or another perform no useful function at all in our society. I certainly would not be in favour of giving them a free ride. I am sure a formula could be devised. I have suggested once or twice it should be 20 per cent of the total vote or 20 per cent of the vote of the successful candidate. I do not think there is anything sacrosanct about 20 per cent. All I say is that no candidate should have his expenses paid unless he gets what you might loosely call a respectable vote, and I would accept almost any definition of any reasonable man or woman as to what that might be. As I say, that is a difficulty. This procedure would certainly make it possible for someone who was an independent candidate, entirely independent of any political party, to represent, as we have seen members in previous parliaments do for long periods of time, important groups of people in this country. No one would want to see them excluded.
I realize that in a very brief explanation of this kind I cannot do any more than give a general idea of what I have in mind. There are just one or two words I have to say in defence of the idea that these expenditures should be paid out of the treasury. I have had some experience in these matters and, although I have never actually collected campaign funds I do not pretend I am entirely unaware of their existence. I am not one of those people who believe that most of the contributors to campaign funds of all parties, with the possible exception of one that is not represented in this house, and I do not mean the Social Credit party, contribute because they really want to further the party and not because of some advantage they are hoping to get for themselves. There are a lot of people who would not agree with that view.

There are many insinuations made about this matter to the effect that contributors to campaign funds really control the party. They are made, I think, by supporters of all parties, but never about their own party. I do not believe really that most of the contributors have that feeling. I am not sure that some of them do not feel they are going to get something out of it for themselves that is not necessarily in the public interest. My point is this: We all know that these expenditures are necessary. We all know that if we are going to have a parliament that is decently representative of the people, these expenses have to be made by candidates and parties. They are really part of the cost of self-government, just as much as the election machinery itself is. It seems to me it is like many of the things that used to be done long ago by charity that are now done by the social services. In this case, we are getting past the point where election campaign funds can be raised solely on a voluntary basis.
Surely, if self-government is worth having, it is worth all of us paying for. It would have this other and final advantage, sir. Every member elected to this parliament, if practically all his election expenses were paid out of the treasury, would undoubtedly have a greater feeling of independence of everyone except his own electors than, at any rate, seems to be the case at the present time. It would remove any suspicion, which is just as important in many ways in these public affairs as anything else, of any member being beholden to any individual or any group in any kind of way except the electorate of his constituency and the people of Canada generally. Well, I think, sir, I have exhausted my time and I have said really all that needs to be said.

I do feel that the committee's work was well done, and this will show up when we next have the act before us.

speechtext:
I appreciate that remark, Mr. Speaker, because I was not sure. I was sure that we had not taken a vote on it.
By way of indicating the common approach to problems by members of that committee, I note that on page 41 of the minutes a motion is recorded as being put by the hon. member for Ottawa East (Mr. Richard) and seconded by myself, and agreed to. Farther along, on the same page, there is recorded a motion put by myself and seconded by the hon. member for Ottawa East. Then, I notice there was a motion moved by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate and seconded by the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard). So, as I say, we did have co-operation in this committee.
I do want to say there is some merit in the resolution we are discussing. However, in view of the fact we so recently overhauled the elections act and we are now trying it out, perhaps we should not consider any large revision at this time. We all agree, I think, that we are very close to an election, and I think it is rather late in the day to be suggesting the government should put up some money for the forthcoming election. For that reason, I do not feel we can reasonably approve of this resolution at the moment.
One of the interesting things about this resolution, Mr. Speaker, is that it comes from a member of the official opposition and not from a member of another party. I noticed in going back over the record of Hansard for a number of years that the members of the C.C.F. party, up until this year, have been putting forward similar suggestions. They have been decrying the fact that the Liberal and Conservative parties were being supported by big business and were saying, in effect, that he who pays the piper calls the tune. I should like to refer to Hansard for July 22, 1958, where the hon. member for Skeena is recorded as saying:
We all know, I am sure, of the Bible phrase, "Where your treasure lies there lies your heart also."
Then further on he says:
I am not saying because they make these contributions that any particular party will perform some sort of skulduggery to ensure that legislation passed is in the interests of the people who

Election Campaign Expenditures make such contributions, but it naturally follows that the party concerned will look upon those who contribute to it as friends and that the legislation it passes will be drafted with this in mind.
Then he goes on:
The general public, in the long run, pays for every political contribution made, whether it be to the Tories or to the Liberals.
I notice that at that time he did not mention his own party.
Later in 1959, when discussing a very similar measure the hon. member for Port Arthur was dealing with the question of contributions to members by political parties and at page 5305 of Hansard of June 30, 1959, he is recorded as saying:
If a political party must count upon secret donations of various kinds I think the thought will always remain in the minds of many people that there are possibilities of undue influence.
We also have other examples of this kind of statement. In 1959, when speaking of the Canada Elections Act, the hon. member for Skeena as reported at page 1953 of Hansard said, and I paraphrase, that we are entitled to know what elements of society, if any, are attempting to subvert political parties. I just point this out to indicate this is an issue that has been pressed for a number of years by the hon. members of the C.C.F. party, that there should not be any contributions, or at least that contributions to party funds should be small. This principle was carried forward into a bill which was presented year after year, until last year. Now it has mysteriously lost favour with the members of the new party, presumably in view of the fact that they are planning and definitely working towards receipt of contributions through a check-off on union dues.
I just mention that in passing because it indicates that a great deal depends on where you sit in how you view these things. A great deal depends on whether you are the recipient of such contributions or whether you cannot get them.
I agree there should be some limitation on what is required by an hon. member to run an election, but if you start drawing a line where will it end? Where do you draw the line in terms of money figures? Every party has a different approach to every campaign in every riding. Every party has a different approach; and you cannot draw a rule for one candidate in a riding which would apply to another candidate in the same riding. If you tried to do that, instead of helping an hon. member you might be restricting him.
You may have an hon. member who has to contend with an opponent who is very well supplied with money. Maybe the money comes legally, maybe it comes illegally; maybe it is spent one way, maybe it is spent another


way; but if large sums of money are being spent to defeat a candidate surely that candidate, if he can, will secure funds to spend an equal amount to hold his seat and try to defeat his opponent?
There is a great deal of merit in the suggestion that is put forward, but I say that for the two reasons I have mentioned, the first being that in such a situation you do not know where to draw the line and the second being that we are shortly approaching another federal election, this would not be a satisfactory time to deal with the matter.

speechtext:
I should like to say a few words on this motion. First of all, may I set the mind of the previous speaker at rest. I do not think it is a very telling argument to suggest that because the party does not put forward a motion it has lost interest in this particular aspect of the problem. I can assure him that the group I am part of would stand by the words he quoted of the hon. member for Skeena and the contribution of the hon. member for Port Arthur. We would still suggest that secret contributions are not the best way of dealing with election expenses.
We still believe in the revelation of all the workings and the financial structures of parties. We still believe this as much as we did before, and therefore I can certainly lend my support to this particular motion. I think it is a good motion and I believe all of us can support it in the sense that it does not suggest any particular change. It simply suggests a consideration and a recommending of means to ensure greater independence to hon. members.
Although it is a little surprising to me that this motion has come forward, nevertheless I think it is perhaps rather interesting and symbolic that it has come forward on the day when elections to the supreme Soviet were announced in the news media. Of course we share popular opinion about this so-called facade of an election whereby people go to the polls to record a ballot for people who have already been hand-picked. It is not so much an election as a verification of candidates; but on the other hand I think we should be concerned that our western, democratic elections should not be in the form of dictatorship. They should not be in the form of dictatorship through news media or control of certain forms of changing opinion in the sense that money does not decide. It is knowledge, integrity, policies and ideas that should really motivate people in recording their votes.
I think we all recognize that an election can be the highest point in our system of

democracy, or it can be the lowest point in that system. All of us are not so naive and completely ignorant of some of the less respectable aspects of our elections, and I think that statement leaves no doubt in any mind as to what is meant by it. Someone has said that we have a parliamentary system which is a good system in spite of, rather than because of, the way we carry on our elections and I believe this is a matter of some concern to a great many people in Canada.
I notice there has been some concern shown over elections and election expenses in the public press, especially in the national magazines. Just last year Mr. James Scott, the former organizer of the Liberal party, wrote a series of articles in the Globe and Mail in which this problem was highlighted.
I do not think this is any time to argue about whose expenses are being gained in a certain way, or who is wrong. The point he made is that all parties should be concerned about this problem of expenses and I believe that the committee proposed would have the advantage of revelation. I do not think there is anything filthy or dirty it is going to reveal. Instead it is going to reveal something very realistic.
I well remember a preacher who once a year would give a sermon, what he called the gospel of gold. He gave this particular sermon every year because he did not want to confuse people with the idea that prayers keep the lights going and fill the furnace in the church. In effect what he was saying is that they had to have money to run a church, and we have to have money to run an election. I think a committee of this sort could put forward some very realistic points which would clear up the misconceptions of people who think that $8 million, $9 million, or $10 million suddenly drop from the heavens in an election year, and we spread this across the nation and elect our candidates. This is an unfortunate misconception which people have. I think it would help all of us in the sense that I am sure everyone of us would like to believe that our parties could be supported by-I am not going to argue this contention today-money coming from government sources. If this were the only money to be used I think this scheme would have some very great merit. Or if it were by contributions openly given by individuals, that would be fine.
I think all of us would like to see our parties run this way. Over the last couple of years there have been a number of articles written on this subject. I do not contend that they are true or false. One was written by Mr. Blair Fraser, and more recently one was 26207-1-123i
Election Campaign Expenditures written by Mr. Peter Newman, indicating where the money was coming from which went to major political parties, to the party that I represent and to the party which is not at this time in the house. In that article he indicated that large corporations were giving very large donations to the same party. Here again there was nothing dirty about it; he simply said that it was there, and really what they were doing was perhaps paying to establish the status quo, or perhaps they were being blackballed into paying for something they did not really want to pay for. However when we get down to it, you and I and every other taxpayer in the country really pays for the election.
